title: Method and caveats
text: This is a record of one economist’s work, kept as the work happened. It is evidence of what an AI agent did in that work, not an estimate of its effect on the team or the industry. Each figure on this site is labelled by where it comes from.

title: Method and caveats
text:
Where the figures come from








Label
Source
Examples




measured
The agent’s session logs, extracted by script
days of use, my turns, agent actions (tool calls), tokens


self-reported
My judgement, entered each week in a spreadsheet and validated by script
hours with AI, hours without AI, confidence, quality, rework, outcome


interpretation
A mapping or reading of the above
the economics-lens channels, the comments under the charts




The unit is the task. One entry per finished piece of work, across all projects.
Hours with AI include prompting, reading and reviewing the agent’s work.
Hours without AI are my estimate of the same task done to the same standard by hand. They are given only for substitution tasks. Expansion tasks have none, because the work would not have been done: their hours are reported as they are.
Confidence in each estimate is mine: high, medium or low. The cautious figure for time saved counts only the tasks where I was highly confident in my estimate and wrote it down within a week of the work.
Which tasks are valued. The weekly log started on 25 September 2026, and its first tasks date from 10 September. Every chart of hours, value types, quality or channels uses those tasks only. Work from June to early September is recorded in the log only as whole-week placeholders, rebuilt from project folders and git history, with no hours or assessment; it appears on this site only through measured usage.
Logged at the time or later. Values written down more than a week after the work are marked backfilled and kept out of the cautious figure.
Usage data starts on 22 July 2026. The agent writes a log of every session and deletes it after about 30 days. The logs were first collected on 8 September 2026, when this record began; by then, sessions before 22 July were gone, and sessions from 22 July to 8 August survive only if they were reopened later. Everything since 8 September is kept.
Not in this report: the text of my assessments, and the content of the work. Projects appear by code (gsma-a, gsma-b, …), and journal revisions show no detail.

title: Method and caveats
text:
What it does not show

Costs. This report is about labour productivity, not about whether the subscription pays for itself.
The team. One worker, who chose to use the tool, on tasks of my own choosing: the selection runs in the tool’s favour.
Effects on output. Time saved is not the same as more or better research; what the saved time went into is not tracked yet.

title: Method and caveats
text:
The case against these results

The strongest objections, and how far the log answers them.

The counterfactual hours are guesses by an interested party. True. They are estimates, made by the person who chose the tool. The log reduces the problem but cannot remove it: estimates are made at the time, with a confidence label, and a cautious figure is shown beside the total. A controlled comparison would be better evidence.
Time saved may be eaten by rework and checking. Rework is logged separately and counted inside my hours, so the time-saved figures are already net of it. Checking time is included in hours with AI.
Expansion work may be work that should not have been done. Some of it may be. Expansion tasks carry no time-saved figure for that reason, and their value rests on what they produce: systems the team now uses, and data that did not exist.
Quality is scored by the person who did the work. Yes. Independent checks exist only inside the systems (second readers, expert reviews), not for the log as a whole.
One enthusiastic early user is not the team. Agreed. This is a case study, useful for what it shows about where agents help and where they fail, not as an estimate of average effects.

title: Method and caveats
section: How the log is kept honest
text:
How the log is kept honest

Every entry is validated by script against a schema before it is accepted; a week’s import writes nothing unless every row passes.
The figures on this site are computed from the log by a script, not typed in.
Shortfalls and below-expectation outcomes are recorded as they happen and shown on the results page.
Corrections to an entry are added as dated updates; nothing is rewritten.

title: Economics lens: measuring productivity
text: Labour economics asks how AI changes work through tasks. Does it take a task over (automation)? Does it make the worker more productive in a task the worker keeps (augmentation, or task complementarity)? Does it create work that did not exist before (new tasks)? This page maps the tasks in my log to those channels. The mapping is my interpretation. The literature draws the line between automation and augmentation in two ways, so both readings are shown.

title: Economics lens: measuring productivity
text:
The task-based view
Acemoglu (2025) sets out four channels through which AI affects production and wages. The other papers this page draws on use the same building blocks.





flowchart TB
    ai["Generative AI and agents"] --> auto["Automation<br/>the task moves to the machine"]
    ai --> comp["Task complementarity<br/>(augmentation)<br/>the worker keeps the task"]
    ai --> deep["Deepening of automation<br/>automated tasks get cheaper"]
    ai --> new["New tasks<br/>work that did not exist"]
    auto --> tfp["Productivity (TFP)"]
    comp --> tfp
    deep --> tfp
    new --> tfp






All four raise productivity, but they act on jobs differently. Automation displaces labour from tasks; complementarity and new tasks raise the demand for it (Acemoglu 2025). Deepening concerns tasks that machines already do, so it does not appear in my log.








Channel
Definition in the literature
Tasks in my log




Automation
AI takes over a task, which is then done “without labor” (Acemoglu 2025; Oleš and Roncone 2026, p. 5).
The research radar and the news radar. They run every day without me. The tasks logged for them are my time building and supervising that automation.


Augmentation (task complementarity)
AI raises the worker’s productivity in a task the worker keeps, including by automating subtasks (Acemoglu 2025); it improves “capabilities, quality, variety, or utility of outputs” (Marguerit 2025, p. 2).
Substitution tasks (same task, less of my time) and quality tasks (same time, better result).


New tasks
New labour-intensive tasks or products (Acemoglu 2025); “new work” (Marguerit 2025, p. 8).
Expansion tasks: work that would not exist without AI.


Skills
Not a separate channel in these papers: Acemoglu places expertise-building inside complementarity.
Learning tasks, shown separately because their value comes later.



The boundary that matters. When an agent writes most of a document and I direct and review it, is that automation or augmentation? Under Acemoglu’s and Oleš and Roncone’s definitions it is augmentation: the task still uses my labour and I remain responsible for it, as with the radiologist who uses AI “while retaining responsibility for the diagnosis” (Oleš and Roncone 2026, p. 1). The Anthropic Economic Index draws the line by interaction instead: work handed over with little back-and-forth counts as automation (Handa et al. 2025). The broad reading below follows that idea. It counts routine, well-specified work I delegated (coding, data analysis, writing, admin) as automation of subtasks.

What the split shows. Under the strict definition, new tasks and augmentation each account for about two fifths of my tasks. New tasks are work that would not have been done at all, and the channel Acemoglu (2025) finds hardest to put numbers on, so estimates built on time savings alone miss them. Automation, the radars, makes up most of the rest. Under the broad definition, much of the augmentation becomes automation of delegated subtasks.

title: Economics lens: measuring productivity
section: Time saved, in the literature’s terms
text:
Time saved, in the literature’s terms
For augmentation tasks that would have happened anyway, the log records the hours with AI and an estimate of the hours without it. That is close to the question Bick, Blandin and Deming (2025, p. 25) ask US workers: “how many additional hours of work would you have needed to complete the same amount of work?” self-reported estimates

subs = entries.filter(d => d.value_type === "substitution" && d.hours_counterfactual !== null)
low = subs.filter(d => d.confidence === "high" && d.logged !== "backfilled")
saving = a => 1 - d3.sum(a, d => d.hours_actual) / d3.sum(a, d => d.hours_counterfactual)
html`<div class="tiles">
  <div class="tile gold"><div class="value">${d3.format(".0%")(saving(subs))}</div><div class="label">of the time these ${subs.length} tasks would have taken was saved (${d3.format(".0%")(saving(low))} on the ${low.length} tasks in the cautious figure)</div></div>
  <div class="tile"><div class="value">27%</div><div class="label">average labour-cost saving per affected task that Acemoglu (2025) takes from experimental studies</div></div>
  <div class="tile"><div class="value">5.4%</div><div class="label">of their work hours saved, on average, by US workers who use generative AI (Bick et al. 2025)</div></div>
</div>`





























These figures are not like for like:

Mine is a saving per task, on tasks I chose to do with an agent.
Acemoglu’s 27% is a saving per affected task, taken from experiments with chatbots (writing and customer support) rather than agents.
Bick et al.’s 5.4% is a share of all of a user’s work hours, including hours spent on tasks AI does not touch.

The direction is still informative. On the tasks it reaches, an agent that can read files, run code and check its own work saves about twice the per-task cost saving in Acemoglu’s estimate. Acemoglu (2025) expects smaller gains on hard tasks without a clear success measure. Much of my work is of that kind, so these figures are evidence on that question, though from a single worker. interpretation

Economics lens: measuring productivity
section: How much I delegate: a measured proxy
text:
How much I delegate: a measured proxy
The Anthropic Economic Index classes interactions as automation when work is handed over with little back-and-forth, and as augmentation when the person iterates, learns or validates (Handa et al. 2025). My session logs allow a measured, if rough, version. measured
How to read the chart. The vertical axis shows how much the agent did for each message I sent. A low value means a conversation: I ask, it answers, I check. A high value means delegation: I hand over a job and the agent carries it out, reading files, running code and searching the web, step after step.

series = [
  {key: "All work", test: d => true},
  {key: "MVNO study (gsma-c)", test: d => d.project === "gsma-c"},
  {key: "Tariff data pipeline (gsma-f)", test: d => d.project === "gsma-f"}
]
monthly = series.flatMap(s => Array.from(d3.rollup(usage.filter(s.test), v => ({turns: d3.sum(v, d => d.human_turns), actions: d3.sum(v, d => d.tool_calls)}), d => d.date.slice(0, 7)),
  ([month, v]) => ({month, series: s.key, ...v, ratio: v.actions / Math.max(v.turns, 1)})))
  .filter(d => d.month >= "2026-08").sort((a, b) => a.month.localeCompare(b.month))
Plot.plot({
  height: 300, width: 720,
  x: {label: null, type: "point", tickFormat: monthName, padding: 0.4},
  y: {label: "Agent actions per message from me", grid: true},
  color: {legend: true, domain: series.map(s => s.key), range: ["#17202a", "#008c95", "#005da8"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(monthly, {x: "month", y: "ratio", stroke: "series", strokeWidth: d => d.series === "All work" ? 3 : 2}),
    Plot.dot(monthly, {x: "month", y: "ratio", fill: "series", r: 5, tip: true,
      title: d => `${monthName(d.month)} · ${d.series}\n${d3.format(",")(d.actions)} agent actions / ${d3.format(",")(d.turns)} messages\n= ${d3.format(".1f")(d.ratio)} per message`}),
    Plot.ruleY([0])
  ]
})























From August, the first full month of surviving logs; November covers 1 to 8 November. Actions include those of helper agents the main agent starts, which is why the tariff pipeline, running many agents in parallel, reaches the highest values.

Across all my work, delegation rose from about 3 agent actions per message in August to about 20 in October. The work moved from asking questions to handing over jobs, towards automation in the broad sense. The tariff pipeline, built to run agents at scale, sits far above the rest. In the MVNO study, delegation rose sharply in November, during the agents’ data collection across markets. This measures how I work, not the economic channel: Anthropic’s own analysis of agentic coding warns that “the boundary between automation and augmentation becomes increasingly blurred with agentic tools”, and the reviewing I do outside a session does not show in it. interpretation

title: Economics lens: measuring productivity
section: What the literature finds, and what I find
text:
What the literature finds, and what I find


Adoption, US
23% of employed US adults used generative AI for work in the week before the survey. Users save 5.4% of their work hours on average, 1.4% of all hours worked, implying a potential productivity gain of about 1.1% (Bick, Blandin and Deming 2025).


Macroeconomics
No more than a 0.66% rise in TFP over ten years, or 0.53% allowing for harder tasks. The gains come from automation and complementarity; new tasks could add more but are hard to measure (Acemoglu 2025).


Automation versus augmentation
The two channels pull in opposite directions. In US local labour markets, a one standard deviation rise in AI automation cuts occupational employment by 21%; the same rise in AI augmentation raises wages by 8% (Oleš and Roncone 2026).


Exposure, UK
94% of UK jobs have some exposure to generative AI and 13% high exposure. Job postings in exposed occupations were about 5.5% lower in 2025-Q2 than pre-ChatGPT trends imply (Henseke et al. 2025).

  <div class="kind" style="font-size:0.8rem;color:#5d6d7e;text-transform:uppercase;letter-spacing:0.04em">My evidence, one economist</div>
  <p style="margin-top:0.5rem">On tasks that would have happened anyway, the agent saved about <b>${d3.format(".0%")(saving(subs))}</b> of the time, roughly twice the per-task saving in Acemoglu's estimate. <b>${d3.format(".0%")(entries.filter(d => d.value_type === "expansion").length / entries.length)}</b> of my tasks would not exist without AI, the radars included. </div>`

title: Generative AI at Work in the Economics Team
text: Since June 2026 I have used Claude Code, an AI agent that reads files, runs code and writes documents, in my work as an economist at GSMA Intelligence. This site reports what I have done with it, what it was worth, and where it fell short, from a log I keep as I work.

title: Generative AI at Work in the Economics Team
text:
Why keep this record

To record the AI work itself. Expanding the team’s AI capability is one of my objectives. The log records every piece of work done with an agent: what it was, how long it took, and how good the result was.
To build a repository of AI-engineering knowledge. Each project records what it learned about building with AI agents: what worked, what failed, and which checks made the agents’ output trustworthy. Those lessons are saved, tested on the next project and turned into a playbook, so that my ability to build AI products improves with each one.
To measure AI at work, as an economist would. The economics of AI asks how it changes tasks, productivity and jobs. My own work is a small, well-documented case: each task is logged with the time it took, an estimate of the time it would have taken without AI, and a quality score.
To share what works with the team. The aim is to help the team judge where agents add value, and where they do not, before deciding how to use them.

title: Generative AI at Work in the Economics Team
Generative AI at Work in the Economics Team
text:
How the evidence is collected





flowchart TB
    work["Work with an AI agent"] --> logs["Session logs<br/>measured: days, messages, agent actions"]
    work --> weekly["Weekly log, every Friday<br/>one row per finished task"]
    logs --> weekly
    weekly --> judge["My judgement per task<br/>hours, hours without AI,<br/>quality, rework, outcome"]
    judge --> ledger["Validated evidence log<br/>one entry per task"]
    ledger --> views["Views: this report,<br/>quarterly reviews"]
    projects["Each project's weekly<br/>lessons on building with agents"] --> kb["Knowledge base and<br/>playbook for new projects"]







Scripts do the counting. Usage figures come from the agent’s session logs, and the weekly table is built by script.
I supply every judgement. Hours, quality and outcome are mine, entered in a spreadsheet each week. Nothing is estimated by the agent.
Failures count. Shortfalls, rework and below-expectation results are logged as they happen and reported here.
Lessons travel. Each project writes down what it has learned about building with agents, and those lessons are distilled into a playbook any new project can start from.

title: Systems built
text: Part of the work went into building systems in which AI agents do work that would not otherwise be done: reading the research and the news every day, rebuilding historical data series, collecting evidence across dozens of countries, answering questions over an economic model. These systems are where most of the new tasks in the log come from. Their value depends on whether their output can be trusted, so each is built around feedback loops that check the agents’ work.

title: Systems built
text:
The systems


System

Data-extraction pipeline
Agents rebuild historical time series from archived web pages and documents, one year per agent, with every value quoted from its source and checked by an independent agent on a different model. Two pilots ran in September; the team approved scaling it up, one country first. Since November it runs on its own agent loop, ready for a wider scope.



System

News radar for the team
An unattended radar that reads public company reporting and the trade press every day, groups coverage into evidence-tiered stories and keeps them in a structured library. A topic expert reviews items through simple forms, and that feedback goes back into the system. Live since late October.



System

Agentic policy simulator
A chat interface over an existing economic model. Questions go to the deterministic model, which produces every figure; the language model only words the answer, and checks reject any figure the model did not produce. Built in June and July 2026.



System

Research radar
Two daily, unattended reviews of new work on AI in the social sciences and in AI engineering. Each development is verified, scored, de-duplicated and archived. Its library feeds the literature behind this report and the method used in the other systems.



Method

Evidence log and playbook
The log behind this site: one validated entry per task, built weekly from the agent’s usage data and my judgements. It also collects each project’s weekly lessons on building with agents into a knowledge base and a public playbook of rules for new projects.



Method

Web search agents for empirical analysis
In the MVNO wholesale access study, agents searched the web to build the treatment variable: MVNO access regulation, by type, for 30 European countries. They also found the market share of MVNOs across Europe. That meant going through hundreds of web pages from different countries, in different languages: work a person could do in principle, but that would not realistically have been done by hand.

title: Systems built
section: How the systems are made trustworthy
text:
How the systems are made trustworthy
Trust comes from feedback loops, not from the model. The method is feedback loop engineering (D. Demmel): agents check their own work against real evidence, independent readers check it again, and every human correction becomes a rule or a check for the next run.





flowchart TB
    rules["Before the work:<br/>schemas, written rules,<br/>restricted inputs"] --> agent["Agent does<br/>the work"]
    agent --> fast["Fast check by script:<br/>every value quoted<br/>from its source"]
    fast -->|errors back as plain text| agent
    fast --> indep["Independent reading<br/>on another model"]
    indep --> recon["Disagreements back<br/>to the agent as a to-do list"]
    recon --> agent
    recon -->|only what stays disputed| human["Human ruling<br/>and spot-check"]
    human --> log["Every intervention<br/>logged"]
    log -->|new rules and checks| rules






What the projects have taught so far is written down as they go. counted from the files



16


weekly handovers from projects on what they learned about building with agents




18


patterns reached independently in two or more projects




17 + 15


core and candidate rules in the playbook for new projects



Some of the lessons that recur:

Judgement to the model, guarantees to code. Anything that must always hold is enforced by a script the agent cannot change, never by an instruction.
Check what is missing, not only what was recorded. Two readers can agree perfectly on a dataset that is missing a whole category. A domain expert found one such gap in a few minutes; sensors for omissions followed.
A failure must never look like an empty result. An aborted step, a stale input or a cut-off file must stop the run loudly.
Count with scripts, not memory. Every figure in a report comes from a command.
